characters: Fatawu: a 12-year-old boy in a white shirt and brown shorts, with a calculator.
Naana: his classmate, 12, in a yellow dress, with a notebook and ruler.
Mr Bonsu: their teacher, in a blue shirt, holding a model pyramid.
The Great Pyramid: a huge stone pyramid of pale blocks in the desert, with workers pulling blocks on sledges.
Merer: an ancient Egyptian work-crew leader in a white kilt, holding a papyrus roll.

narrationPlan.voice: Clear, amazed storyteller voice; Mr Bonsu is energetic and precise
narrationPlan.pace: Clear and amazed, with an expert tone (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Warm desert strings and a steady drum, rising for the discoveries (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The Great Pyramid is in Egypt, in Africa, so pupils can connect it with their own continent’s history. The pupils and teacher here are invented.
The story stresses that people built the pyramid and does not suggest that it was made by magic or visitors from space.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check the facts against a named source: height 147 m (original), about 2.3 million blocks of 2.5 to 15 tonnes, built over roughly 20 years, Wadi al-Jarf papyri found 2011 to 2013 by Pierre Tallet’s team, a 64 km Nile branch (Eman Ghoneim’s radar study) beside about 31 pyramids, and a cavity above the Grand Gallery.
The crew leader’s name Merer comes from general knowledge; the Science Focus page used did not name him. Verify.
Check the maths: 2.3 million blocks over 20 years is 115,000 a year, about 315 a day, about 13 an hour for 24 hours.

teacherGuide.overview: A mostly solved mystery that shows how new tools (a logbook, satellite radar) answer old questions. Some parts, such as how blocks were lifted, remain debated, and a hidden space is still unknown.
learningGoals: Explain what archaeologists use as evidence.
Separate solved, debated and unknown parts of the story.
Use rates and division to understand a large project.
beforeReading: Ask: how many blocks would you need to build a tower the size of our classroom?
whileReading: At page 2, ask learners to check the maths on blocks per day.
afterReading: Build a model pyramid from paper or blocks.
Debate: which part of the mystery is most interesting?
discussion: Why is “who built it” different from “how was it lifted”?
reflection: What would you want to ask Merer?

mathsExtension.task: 2.3 million blocks in 20 years: about how many blocks a year?
About how many blocks a day (365 days)?
About how many blocks an hour, if work went on 24 hours a day?

support: Provide a calculator and a table: year, day, hour.
stretch: Investigate how a team of workers might be organised into crews.

culturalNotes: The Great Pyramid is in Egypt, in Africa, so pupils can connect it with their own continent’s history. The pupils and teacher here are invented.
The story stresses that people built the pyramid and does not suggest that it was made by magic or visitors from space.
localiseThis: Connect Egypt to Africa on a map and to Ghana’s own history of large building projects.
Do not suggest or accept “aliens built it”; emphasise evidence for human builders.

whatWeKnow: The Great Pyramid was built more than 4,000 years ago by organised crews.
A logbook and a lost branch of the Nile show that boats helped move stone.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact methods used to lift the blocks.
What the cavity above the Grand Gallery is for.
How construction was organised in detail.

factCheck.claim: The Great Pyramid was originally 147 m tall and has about 2.3 million blocks of 2.5 to 15 tonnes; Pierre Tallet’s team found logbook papyri at Wadi al-Jarf (2011 to 2013); Eman Ghoneim’s team found a 64 km ancient branch of the Nile beside 31 pyramids; the lifting method is debated; the purpose of a cavity above the Grand Gallery is unclear.
factCheck.reference: BBC Science Focus, “We might finally know how the pyramids were built.”
